passage: I'm Thomas, and I'm ten. On Sports Day, my best friend Chinmay won the drawing competition. His picture of rain on our school roof got first prize. When they called his name, I clapped so hard my hands went red. I shouted "Chinmay!" so loudly that the teacher looked at me. I was really, really happy for him. He had practised every lunch break. But when I saw my own drawing on the board with no ribbon, I felt a small pinch inside. I wanted a ribbon too. Both feelings were there at the same time. After school we shared his prize chocolate on the steps, and the pinch mostly went away.

qa.q: What was Chinmay's winning picture of?
qa.a: Rain on the school roof.

qa.q: What two feelings did Thomas have at the prize-giving?
qa.a: Real happiness for Chinmay, clapping till Thomas's hands went red, and a small pinch of wanting a ribbon too.

qa.q: What helped the pinch go away, and what does that show?
qa.a: Sharing the prize chocolate with Chinmay on the steps; staying close to a friend made room for both the joy and the small wish.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt hearing Thomas shout his name?
qa.a: Chinmay probably felt proud and cared for, knowing his best friend was truly happy for him 😊

grounding: A child cheers loudly for a friend's prize and feels warm joy alongside a small pang of wanting one too.

passage: Class 4 note, spelling bee day. By Sharmila, class teacher. When Rhea won the final round, the loudest clapping came from Rhea's best friend, Minakshi, who had been knocked out in round three. Minakshi jumped up, clapped above her head and hugged Rhea before Rhea had even collected the trophy. A minute later I saw her look at the trophy and then down at her shoes, just for a moment. I think a small pang was there too, and that is natural. At break I told Minakshi, "You were a wonderful friend today. And round three was hard. Want to practise some tricky words together next week?" She grinned and said yes. I'll keep two lunch breaks free.

qa.q: In which round was Minakshi knocked out?
qa.a: Round three.

qa.q: What does Minakshi looking at the trophy and then at her shoes suggest?
qa.a: Alongside real joy for Rhea, she may have felt a small pang of wishing she had won too.

qa.q: How did Sharmila respond to both of Minakshi's feelings?
qa.a: Sharmila praised her as a wonderful friend, said round three was hard, and offered practice together, so both the joy and the wish were respected.

qa.q: What was it like for Rhea to be hugged by Minakshi before collecting the trophy?
qa.a: Rhea likely felt extra happy and supported, knowing a friend who had been knocked out was celebrating so warmly.

grounding: A teacher notes a girl cheering her best friend's win with real joy while a small pang shows for a moment.

passage: Saturday. Dear diary, Kishore won the inter-school chess tournament today!!! I was there when he checkmated the boy from the other school. I jumped up and clapped so loud the arbiter said "Shh!" I didn't care. Kishore taught me chess in Class 3, so it's like half my win too. 😊 Okay, truth: when they gave him the big trophy, I felt a tiny bit jealous. I lost in round two. I wanted to be up there. But mostly I was proud. Both feelings are true, I think. Tomorrow I'm asking him to teach me the move he used. Ujjwal

qa.q: In which round did Ujjwal lose?
qa.a: Round two.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when Kishore got the big trophy?
qa.a: Mostly proud, with a tiny bit of jealousy at wanting to be up there too.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal plan for tomorrow, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: To ask Kishore to teach the winning move, turning the small jealousy into learning and time together.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel about Ujjwal's loud clapping?
qa.a: Kishore would likely feel happy and supported, especially as he taught Ujjwal chess back in Class 3.

grounding: A child cheers Kishore's chess win with real pride, while admitting a tiny pang of jealousy.

passage: At the Pola fair in Kinhi, the school's rangoli contest was judged under the big neem. Preeti, ten, had drawn a peacock. Her best friend Vijay had made a bullock pair in orange and green, every bell drawn with a matchstick. When the headmaster read out, "First prize, Vijay Wankhede!" Preeti jumped up and clapped so hard her bangles clinked. "Vijay! Vijay!" He went pink and grinned at her. She was glad, truly glad; he had practised on his courtyard floor for a week. Then she glanced at her peacock, with no ribbon beside it, and something small pinched inside. She wished there had been a ribbon for her too. But when Vijay ran over with his prize, she grabbed his arm and swung it high, laughing.

qa.q: What did Vijay draw for the rangoli contest?
qa.a: A bullock pair in orange and green, with every bell drawn with a matchstick.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she glanced at her own peacock?
qa.a: A small pinch of wishing for a ribbon, sitting alongside her real gladness for Vijay.

qa.q: What could Preeti say to herself about the pinch she felt?
qa.a: That wanting a prize herself is normal and doesn't cancel her happiness for Vijay; she could practise her peacock for next year.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel with Preeti cheering loudest?
qa.a: Vijay probably feels shy but very happy, with his best friend celebrating his win so openly.

grounding: A child cheers her friend's prize with real warmth while a small wish for herself sits underneath.

passage: In the school hall in Rotterdam, the poetry prize was the last thing announced before the holidays. Elif, eleven, had written about her grandmother's garden. Her best friend Vera had written about the sea. When Mr Jansen said, "The winner is Vera Kowalczyk!" Elif was the first on her feet, clapping and whistling, which she'd only just learned to do. Vera went bright red. Elif felt warm all over; she'd heard Vera read that poem aloud on the tram and knew it was good. Then, as Vera walked up for the book token, Elif thought of her own poem, still folded in her bag, and a small ache came and sat quietly beside the warmth. On the way out, she hugged Vera anyway. "Read it to me again on the tram?"

qa.q: What did Vera's winning poem describe?
qa.a: Vera wrote about the sea.

qa.q: What shows that Elif feels real warmth for Vera, even with the small ache?
qa.a: She's first on her feet, whistling, and hugs Vera afterwards asking to hear the poem again; the ache sits beside the warmth rather than replacing it.

qa.q: What small step could Elif take with her own folded poem?
qa.a: She could share it with Vera on the tram too, or ask Mr Jansen for feedback, turning her wish into her next try.

qa.q: How might Vera feel hearing Elif's whistle first?
qa.a: Vera probably feels embarrassed but delighted, knowing her best friend is proud of her.

grounding: A child cheers her friend's win with genuine warmth while a small wish for herself sits beneath.

passage:
Tuesday
Today Rafiq won first prize in the district drawing competition! His picture of the fish market with all the crows. I clapped so hard my hands went red. I even whistled, and Ma'am gave me a look.
I felt happy all the way up to my ears. Rafiq's my best friend and he draws every single day, even in maths class.
But also, when they said his name, a little part of me went "what about me?" My picture was the train. I worked on it for two weeks.
I think both feelings were there at the same time. The happy one was bigger.
After school we shared his prize chocolate. He gave me the bigger half.
– Nilesh

qa.q: What did Rafiq draw?
qa.a: The fish market with all the crows.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when Rafiq's name was called?
qa.a: Nilesh felt very happy for Rafiq, and also a small pang of wanting a prize too.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do with the "what about me?" feeling?
qa.a: Nilesh could keep drawing the train pictures, and maybe ask Rafiq for tips, letting the wish push Nilesh on instead of spoiling the happy feeling.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel about Nilesh's clapping?
qa.a: Rafiq probably felt proud and loved, seeing his best friend cheer so loudly for him.

grounding: It shows a child clapping loudly for a friend's prize, feeling warmth with a small pang beneath.

passage:
On sports day at the village school near Hosur, the dust rose in yellow clouds. Tanvir, eleven, had come fourth in the 100 metres. His legs still stung.
Then came the 400 metres. His friend Jeevan, the smallest boy in the class, started slow and then flew past everyone on the last bend.
Tanvir leapt up. "JEEVAN! JEEVAN!" He clapped hard.
When Jeevan came to the steps, gasping, holding the tin medal, Tanvir thumped his back. "You were like a rocket!"
Later, sitting under the tamarind tree, Tanvir looked at the medal in Jeevan's hand. He felt a little tug inside. He wanted one too.
But the tug was small, and the happy feeling was big. "Next year we both get one," he said.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir and Jeevan sit later?
qa.a: Under the tamarind tree.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he looked at the medal under the tree?
qa.a: He felt a small tug of wanting a medal too, alongside a much bigger happiness for Jeevan.

qa.q: What small step could help Tanvir with that little tug?
qa.a: He could practise with Jeevan for next year, turning the wish into a shared goal, as his words suggest.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel with Tanvir cheering for him?
qa.a: Jeevan probably felt proud and supported, having a friend thump his back and call him a rocket.

grounding: It shows a child cheering loudly for a friend's win and feeling warmth, with a small pang of wanting beneath.

passage:
The school hall in Lisbon was full of parents, and Beatriz, nine, sat in the front row with her class. Her friend Emeka stood at the microphone for the last word of the spelling bee.
"Necessary."
Emeka closed his eyes. "N-E-C-E-S-S-A-R-Y."
The bell rang. He'd won.
Beatriz jumped up clapping so loudly that her shoes squeaked on the chair. She had been knocked out in round three, on "rhythm". For one second, watching him hold the silver cup, she wished it were her hands on it. The wish pinched a little.
Then Emeka looked straight at her and grinned, and the pinch was gone under a big warm feeling. She had helped him practise all week at lunch.
"You did it!" she shouted over everyone.

qa.q: Which word did Emeka spell to win?
qa.a: "Necessary".

qa.q: What was Beatriz feeling as Emeka held the cup?
qa.a: She felt a small pinch of wishing she had won, then a big warm happiness for her friend.

qa.q: How could a teacher support both children after the spelling bee?
qa.a: A teacher could praise Emeka's win and also notice Beatriz's kindness in helping him practise and cheering, so both feel seen.

qa.q: What was it like for Emeka to see Beatriz cheering?
qa.a: He probably felt happy and supported, grinning straight at the friend who had helped him practise.

grounding: It shows a child cheering loudly for a friend's win, feeling warmth with a small pang beneath.

passage:

As she walked to the stage, Madhav felt warm all over, as if he had won too. Under the warmth sat a tiny pinch: his own drawing hadn't been mentioned. He noticed it and let it sit there.
When Afreen came back holding her certificate, he said, "I knew it! The peacock's tail was the best part." Then, more quietly, "Can you show me how you did the feathers?"

passage:
Monday: Pema and Pranav both entered the inter-school quiz and practised together every recess.
Friday, quiz day: Pema was knocked out in the second round. Pranav went on and won. When they called his name, Pema cheered so loudly the teacher laughed, and she hugged him in the corridor. On the bus home, though, she stared out of the window for a while. She had wanted to win too.
Saturday: Pema made Pranav a card with a gold star and wrote, "Best quiz partner ever. Next year, both of us in the final." She felt good giving it. The little ache was still there, but smaller, sitting next to the happy part.

qa.q: In which round was Pema knocked out?
qa.a: The second round.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling on the bus home?
qa.a: She felt a quiet ache of disappointment, wishing she had won too, even though she was happy for Pranav.

qa.q: What did Pema do that let both feelings live together?
qa.a: She made Pranav a card celebrating him and set a goal for both of them next year.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel receiving the card?
qa.a: He would likely feel touched and happy that his friend is proud of him.

grounding: Shows a child cheering a friend's quiz win with real warmth while a small wish for herself sits alongside, over several days.

passage:
Naveen, you clapped the loudest when your friend won the chess prize, but you look a little quiet now. Let your Anirban dadu tell you something. When I was ten, in Kolkata, my best friend Biswa won the swimming race at the pujo sports. I jumped on the bench and shouted his name till my throat hurt. I was so happy for him, truly.
But that night, in bed, I felt a small ache too. I had practised in the pond all summer. Both feelings were true, and I didn't have to choose between them. The next morning I asked Biswa to teach me his turn. He did. We swam together for fifty years.
So, which feeling is bigger right now?

qa.q: Which race did Biswa win?
qa.a: The swimming race at the pujo sports.

qa.q: What did young Anirban feel that night in bed?
qa.a: He felt a small ache of disappointment alongside his real joy for Biswa.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned the ache into something good?
qa.a: Asking Biswa to teach him his turn the next morning.

qa.q: How might Biswa have felt when Anirban cheered?
qa.a: Biswa probably felt proud and loved, hearing his best friend shout his name.

grounding: A grandfather recalls cheering his best friend's win with real joy while a small ache for himself sat underneath, and both feelings being true.

passage: The prize-giving was held on the hottest day of May, and the fans in the school hall had stopped working. Wasim sat sweating in the third row. When the principal called 'Zeenat Hussain, first prize, essay writing!', Wasim clapped so hard his hands stung. Zeenat was his best friend. She'd read him her essay on the bus every day for a week. Under his clapping, though, there was a tiny pang. He had entered too, and his name wasn't called. He noticed it, like a pebble in his shoe. But when Zeenat came back holding the certificate, he grinned and said, 'Told you!' The pang was still there, a little. So was the warm, happy feeling. Both at the same time.

qa.q: Which prize did Zeenat win?
qa.a: First prize in essay writing.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling while he clapped?
qa.a: Wasim felt warm and happy for Zeenat, with a tiny pang underneath because his own name wasn't called.

qa.q: What could a teacher say to children who feel both happy and a little sad at prize-giving?
qa.a: The teacher could say it's normal to feel both, and that being glad for a friend while wishing for yourself is okay.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel hearing Wasim say 'Told you!'?
qa.a: Zeenat would likely feel happy and supported, knowing her friend believed in her.

grounding: A child claps hard when a friend wins a prize and feels warmth, with a small pang of wishing for himself beneath it.

passage: The Christmas term science fair at the Delhi school ended with the results. When Dhruv's name was read out for first prize, Jyoti jumped up and clapped louder than anyone. She had helped him paint the volcano. Her own project, the water filter, got a 'good effort' sticker. For a moment, walking back to her seat, she felt a pang, like a pinch. She would have liked her name to be called too. But then Dhruv ran over and hugged her. 'Your red paint won it!' Jyoti laughed, and the warm feeling was bigger than the pinch. At home she told Mumma, 'I'm so happy for Dhruv. And I want to win next year.'

qa.q: What sticker did Jyoti's project get?
qa.a: A 'good effort' sticker.

qa.q: What did Jyoti feel walking back to her seat?
qa.a: Jyoti felt a small pang, wishing her own name had been called, alongside her happiness for Dhruv.

qa.q: How could Mumma respond to Jyoti's words at home?
qa.a: Mumma could say both feelings make sense and help her plan a project she's excited about for next year.

grounding: A child claps for a friend's win and feels warmth, with a small pang underneath; happiness for another sits beside a wish for herself.

passage:
'Gargi! Did you hear? Sarita won the Onam drawing competition!'
'Really?' Gargi ran to the gate. 'SARITA! You won!'
Sarita came running up the lane, waving a certificate. 'First prize!'
'I knew it! Your elephant was the best!' Gargi hugged her so hard they both fell over laughing.
Amma came to the door. 'Gargi, you entered too, no?'
'Yes, Amma.'
'Are you sad?'
Gargi thought. 'A little bit. Here.' She touched her tummy. 'But mostly I'm happy. She practised every day.'
'Both is fine,' said Amma.
Sarita looked at Gargi. 'Next year, you'll win.'
'Maybe we'll both win,' Gargi said.

qa.q: What did Sarita win?
qa.a: The Onam drawing competition, first prize.

qa.q: What does Gargi touching her tummy show about her feelings?
qa.a: It shows she felt a little sad about not winning, even though she was mostly happy for Sarita.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped Gargi?
qa.a: Amma asked gently how she felt and said 'Both is fine', letting Gargi hold happiness and sadness together.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel when Gargi hugs her?
qa.a: Sarita probably feels proud and loved, sharing her win with a friend who is truly glad.

grounding: A child celebrates a friend's prize with real warmth, while a small pang of wishing for herself sits beneath it.

passage: Last Saraswati Puja our para had a drawing contest, and I, Irawati, was sure my peacock would win. Arnab drew the river behind his house, with a boat and a tiny dog on the bank. When they called his name for first prize, I clapped so hard my palms stung. I even whistled, which Ma says is rude. Arnab looked back at me and grinned, holding his certificate as if it might fly away. I was so happy for him. But on the walk home, a small part of me kept thinking about my peacock. Both feelings were there together, like two sweets in one box.

qa.q: What did Arnab draw?
qa.a: The river behind his house, with a boat and a tiny dog on the bank.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling during the prize announcement and on the walk home?
qa.a: Irawati felt real joy for Arnab, clapping till the palms stung, and later a small pang of disappointment about the peacock.

qa.q: What would you tell Irawati about having both feelings?
qa.a: That it is normal to be happy for a friend and still wish you had won; the pang can even become a goal for next year's contest.

qa.q: How did Arnab seem to take Irawati's loud clapping?
qa.a: Arnab looked back and grinned, so the cheering likely made him feel proud and supported by a friend.

grounding: A child cheers a friend's prize with warmth while a small pang of wanting to win sits underneath.
